name: Sortd
tagline: A small paid iOS app for sorting and tidying stuff on your phone into buckets.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is a single-purpose iOS utility, and the logic inside single-purpose iOS utilities is almost always trivial: a list, some buckets, a swipe gesture, local storage. An agent will write that in one sitting and it will work. The gap is everything around the logic: getting it onto your phone means Xcode, a signing profile, and a rebuild every seven days unless you pay Apple 99 a year for a developer account. Gesture feel, haptics, and the thousand small animation decisions that make a swipe-to-sort app pleasant are also the part agents are worst at. So: buildable, but you are trading a few quid for a weekend and a permanently slightly worse feel.
coreLoopDIY: A local SwiftUI app that shows you one item at a time and lets you swipe it into user-defined buckets, with undo and a review screen, all stored on device.
requirements: An Apple ID for local signing, or a paid developer account if you want the build to last longer than seven days
An iPhone for anything gesture-based, since the simulator lies about feel
whatYouLose: Installation that takes ten seconds instead of an afternoon of provisioning profiles
iCloud sync across your devices, unless you add CloudKit and debug it
Widgets, Shortcuts actions, and Share Sheet integration, which are each their own small project
Gesture polish and haptics tuned by someone who shipped and iterated on this
Updates when iOS breaks something, which it will
moatNotes: The moat on cheap iOS utilities is not technology, it is that the App Store makes buying frictionless and self-signing makes DIY annoying forever.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a one-time App Store purchase is cheaper than a weekend, and because the distribution asymmetry never goes away. Even a perfect clone has to be re-signed and re-installed on a schedule, and it will never appear in a widget or a Shortcut without more work. People pay small money for small apps precisely to avoid owning the maintenance.
notes: The code is a weekend; the install pipeline is the tax you keep paying.
prompt:
Build a local-only iOS app called Triage: a swipe-to-sort utility for working through a backlog of items one at a time.

Stack, no substitutions:
- SwiftUI, iOS 17 minimum
- SwiftData for persistence, single local store, no CloudKit
- No networking, no accounts, no analytics, no third-party packages

Data model:
- Bucket: id, name, colour hex, sortOrder
- Item: id, title, optional note, createdAt, bucket (optional, nil means unsorted)
- Seed three buckets on first launch: Keep, Later, Bin

Screens:
1. Sort: shows the oldest unsorted Item as a card. Swipe right to assign the first bucket, left for the second, up for the third. Show bucket name and colour as the card moves so the user knows where it is going. Card springs back if the drag is released under threshold.
2. Buckets: list of buckets with item counts, tap to see contents, swipe a row to delete or rename a bucket. Deleting a bucket sets its items back to unsorted.
3. Add: a text field plus a done button that creates an unsorted Item and keeps focus for fast entry.

Behaviour:
- Undo: a floating button that reverses the last assignment, keep a stack of at least twenty actions in memory
- Haptic feedback on assignment, light impact
- Empty state on Sort screen when nothing is unsorted, with a button to the Add screen
- Everything works offline and in airplane mode because there is no network code

Out of scope, do not build: sign in, sharing, widgets, Shortcuts, iCloud sync, onboarding tour, paywall.

Deliver an Xcode project that builds and runs in the simulator, plus a README with the exact steps to install it on a physical iPhone with a free Apple ID, including the note that free signing expires after seven days.
